withheld.headline: Bangladesh flood death toll rises to 44 as more than one million people affected
withheld.evidence: Relentless monsoon rains, flash floods and landslides have left at least 44 people dead and affected more than one million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, authorities said on Sunday, as emergency responders continued relief operations amid warnings of further flooding. According to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, more than 1.022 million people have been affected by the flooding, with 267,918 families remaining stranded by rising waters. At least 39 people have been injured since the severe weather began. The worst-hit districts include Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, where floodwaters have inundated 58 sub-districts (upazilas), damaging homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure. Although rainfall eased over the past 24 hours in several parts of the country, flood risks remain elevated. The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) warned that fresh short-term flooding could occur in Feni, Sylhet and northern districts, particularly along the Teesta River basin, due to continued upstream inflows and additional rainfall. The agency said water levels at seven monitoring stations on the Sangu, Matamuhuri, Kushiyara, Manu and Someswari rivers remained above danger levels, keeping low-lying communities at risk. Authorities have opened 1,131 emergency shelters, where 44,457 displaced people are currently staying after being evacuated from flood-affected areas. The Disaster Management Ministry said it had allocated 145 million taka ($1.2 million) and 2,650 metric tonnes of rice to the seven worst-hit districts to support relief efforts. Since July 7, district administrations across the country have also received 345 million taka and 6,900 metric tonnes of rice for emergency response operations. withheld.headline: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional | CBC News
withheld.evidence: The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. This was the second time the province of Alberta had challenged the act, which sets out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines. In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction. "While Parliament may have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the [Impact Assessment Act] creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects," the court wrote. Canada's top court rules environmental impact law unconstitutional "This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, on the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction." The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren't constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction. "The decision maker may regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project," the court wrote. withheld.headline: Why returning to Syria is only the first step toward rebuilding lives shattered by war
withheld.evidence: WASHINGTON D.C.: When Jihan Hamad Al-Khalaf and her extended family decided to leave Turkiye and return to Syria, there was little debate among them. Five of the seven related families had been away since 2013, while the other two left in 2018. Some of their children had only faint memories of Syria, while others had never seen it. Yet after the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in December 2024, Al-Khalaf said their decision was “immediate and collective.” “Conditions and pressures in Turkiye helped accelerate the decision,” the Syrian journalist and humanitarian activist told Arab News. “But the main reason was that the country had been liberated and the war was over.” The children, raised on their parents’ memories of Syria, were among the most enthusiastic. The first family returned in January 2025. Their story is part of one of the largest recent return movements in the world. UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, estimated that about 1.82 million Syrians had returned from abroad between Dec. 8, 2024, and Oct. Lebanon accounted for the largest number of returns in that estimate, at about 733,000, followed by Turkiye with about 713,000. A separate UNHCR crisis tally recorded about 1.08 million Syrian arrivals from Lebanon by Sept. 30, following the regional escalation that began in late February. Some 91 percent of respondents said essential services were missing in their communities, 71 percent were living in damaged housing, and only 18 percent said they had received adequate support during the return process. During the first winter, two families lived together in one room. As relatives found work, they slowly installed windows, doors, and electricity. When refugees in Turkiye ask her about conditions in Syria, she tells them that what they see will depend partly on what they expect. “If you put on rose-tinted glasses, you will see that returning is suitable and everything is good,” she said.

withheld.headline: Burkina Faso to Kasoa on Foot: Man completes 22-day anti-galamsey march
withheld.evidence: Marathon walker, King Klottey, has successfully completed his remarkable 22-day cross-border trek from Burkina Faso to Kasoa, aimed at raising public consciousness over the destruction and pollution of Ghana's major water bodies. In viral footage circulating online, and sighted by GhanaWeb on October 11, 2026, Klottey was seen arriving in Kasoa, flanked by supporters waving flags and security personnel, to mark the end of his grueling journey. The activist undertook the multi-week walk to draw urgent attention to environmental degradation, illegal mining (galamsey), and toxic contamination threatening river systems and drinking water sources across West Africa. Throughout his trek from the Burkinabe border through several Ghanaian towns, King Klottey engaged local residents and climate conscious youth on the imperative need to protect aquatic ecosystems and hold environmental polluters accountable. Illegal small-scale mining (galamsey) remains one of Ghana's most pressing socio-ecological challenges, leading to widespread heavy metal pollution in key river basins such as the Pra, Ankobra, Birim, and Densu.

withheld.headline: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
withheld.evidence: A famous Scottish fossil is forcing scientists to rethink what claw-like feet really reveal about the move onto land. Pressed flat inside two slabs of Scottish rock, a 345-million-year-old skeleton seemed to carry some unmistakable signs of life on land. Its four limbs ended in five-digit feet, and the tips of its fingers and toes looked strikingly like claws. For decades, those features helped make Westlothiana lizziae , better known as “Lizzie,” a landmark in the story of how vertebrates moved away from water and gave rise to reptiles, birds, and mammals. Yet the fossil had been crushed so badly that much of its anatomy remained hidden inside the stone. Peering through that rock with X-rays has now exposed a very different animal. Researchers from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, reconstructed structures that could not be seen from the fossil’s surface. “Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades,” said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum’s Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. “But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected.” Discovered in Scotland in 1984 and formally described in 1990, Westlothiana had initially been interpreted largely from the anatomy exposed on the surfaces of its two slabs. From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two. Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort. But research into the life story of Vanke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers. About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945. After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow. The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators. withheld.headline: Mississauga mayoral candidates talk redeveloping Living Arts Centre, platform policy planks
withheld.evidence: With two-and-a-half weeks to go until Mississauga election day, talk about potentially redeveloping a notable chunk of the city’s downtown entered into the campaign on Thursday as mayoral candidates put forward various policy ideas and focuses. While unveiling the remaining parts of her campaign platform, Bonnie Crombie said she wants to put a stop to studying the potential demolition of the Living Arts Centre as part of a massive redevelopment project. “I will cancel Carolyn Parrish’s proposed redevelopment of the Living Arts Centre and surrounding civic lands, a $2.5-billion vanity project at a time when residents are struggling with everyday bills; this is the wrong priority,” she told reporters, arguing any potential municipal funding should be redirected to other priorities and initiatives. The Living Arts Centre, located just north of Mississauga city hall and west of Square One, opened in 1997. It has a 1,300-seat main auditorium along with various meeting rooms and exhibition spaces. Earlier in 2026, Mississauga city council voted to begin a study and consultation process that could ultimately result in a downtown transformation. The major part of the planning centres around potentially replacing the Living Arts Centre and a nearby park, which totals around 12 acres, with a new convention centre, hotel, music hub, offices, apartments and retail spaces. “The mayor’s plan to build a $2.5-billion convention centre is a terrible idea; no one is asking for this. They’re also going to be taking out the parkland and the parking in the area. That green space is so valued for the residents who live in that area,” he said, adding he wants residents to help determine the future for the area and is open to potentially renovating the Living Arts Centre. “I will put the priorities of Mississaugans first and they’re clear: To bring taxes under control, protect jobs, attract investment, get Mississauga moving again and make our neighbourhoods safer,” she said. “Here [are] the highlights of my plan: Freeze property taxes in 2027 and thereafter keep them at or below inflation, stop the waste at city hall (and) hire an independent auditor general, stop the $100 million that we’re bleeding every year to Brampton by fixing the unfair policing formula, (and) allowing ‘six-plexes’ as of right on certain arterial roads to make housing more affordable and realistic for young families,” she said Thursday afternoon. When asked what she wanted to accomplish if she gets elected for a full term, Parrish said she was focused on two areas. “Housing, I want to keep that up. I was at a topping-off ceremony yesterday for three towers on the other side of Port Credit. This is a ground-breaker, and it’s all because of the incentive that we brought in as a council,” she said Thursday afternoon, adding the changes have resulted in support from developers.

withheld.headline: The animal kingdom may be 800 million years old: Mongolia removes a ceiling from the molecular clock
withheld.evidence: A team from Oxford, Berkeley, Zurich and Yale places the origin of animals between 800 and 700 million years ago, 126 to 226 million years before the oldest animal fossils. The argument rests on an absence in a Mongolian rock, not on a new fossil. The study appeared in Science Advances on 2 October 2026. The dates in play for the origin of animals, in millions of years ago: the molecular-clock estimate of Lole Durbin et al., the deposits proposed as a maximum limit, the Kheseen Biota, the biomarkers, the Weng’an Biota and the earliest animal fossils. Ages and localities marked with an asterisk come from the University of Oxford press release. Chart produced by ScienceOnline from data in Lole Durbin O.M. et al., Science Advances 2026, doi 10.1126/sciadv.aeg6289. Image file: 2026-10-08_02_grafico_en.png In Mongolia there is a rock that preserves microfossils exceptionally well. It is called the Kheseen Biota and it formed between 550 and 526 million years ago, when animals certainly existed. It holds no definite animal.That absence is the starting point of a study by Orin Lole Durbin, Eliel Anttila, Derek Briggs, Francis Macdonald and Ross Anderson, published in Science Advances on 2 October 2026. Lole Durbin is first author. The team includes researchers from Berkeley, ETH Zurich and Yale.The problem is one of dates. Lipid biomarkers, fossil molecules left by cell membranes, point to animals before 635 million years ago. Anderson concedes that the birth date of the animal kingdom will stay uncertain until older fossils turn up. withheld.headline: Concerns as Residents Eat Fish From Fuel-hit River Nyando Following Leak
withheld.evidence: Kenya, 11 October 2026 - Some residents of the villages neighbouring the riverbanks of the River Nyando in Kisumu County are eating fish caught after fuel leaked into the water from a Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) line. Health concerns are mounting, while Kisumu Governor Prof Anyang’ Nyong’o on Friday demanded an impartial investigation into the fuel leak. The leak, reported on 8 October 2026, occurred on the Sinendet-Kisumu petroleum pipeline, which runs beside the river near Muhoroni, Kibigori and Ahero. Some locals risked their lives trying to collect fuel floating on the water. Others have since been catching and eating fish from the affected stretch. In their initial response, KPC officials suspected that the leak was caused by intentional interference with the line. They have since alerted detectives from the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) and the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) to investigate and arrest any culprits. It was first reported that the pipeline was damaged while workers dug to build gabions on the riverbank to curb erosion ahead of the El Niño rains. Between 2009 and 2018 alone, about 65,000 people died as a result of technological events. Fuels also contain benzene, for which Kenya’s Onshore National Contingency Plan sets a worker exposure limit of 1 part per million over eight hours. According to scientific researchers, teleost fish can metabolise PAHs efficiently, breaking them down and excreting them. This typically leaves lower residues in their edible flesh than in shellfish and, in principle, reduces the risk to people who eat them. That does not make fish from fuel-affected water safe.

withheld.headline: Bass-led turnout surge crashes meeting to replace L.A. homeless outreach agency
withheld.evidence: It's not unusual for a public meeting to be canceled for lack of a quorum. But there isn't even a word for what happened Friday when a once-obscure board canceled a meeting to decide the future of homeless services in Los Angeles because too many people came to vote. More than 1,500 potential voters signed up for a meeting of the Los Angeles Continuum of Care board to pick a replacement for the core duties of the beleaguered Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority. Under the board's unusual charter, they all were eligible to vote merely because of their interest in homelessness. The onslaught was organized by Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who sent out a blast message through her communications networks urging people to join the meeting via Zoom to vote down the board's recommendation that Los Angeles County assume those duties. The response was overwhelming, but it didn't work. Over cries of foul from those who came in person, the board's attorney Shayla Myers announced the meeting was canceled because the Zoom channel had a capacity of only 1,000. LAHSA contested the move in federal court. The county has committed that the City of Los Angeles would "at a minimum" maintain its access to the database and matching system, Horvath said. Times staff writer David Zahniser contributed to this report.

withheld.headline: OrbitalHub » CHIME detects cosmic hydrogen on its own
withheld.evidence: Direct any inquiries to contact@orbitalhub.com. The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment, run out of a low-slung cluster of wire-mesh cylinders near Penticton, British Columbia, has just done something the rest of cosmology has been waiting on for the better part of two decades. In a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal on 28 September 2026 and posted to arXiv as 2511.19620, the CHIME Collaboration reports the first standalone detection of the cosmological 21-centimeter signal, the faint radio glow of neutral hydrogen from an era when the universe was roughly five billion years old. The result reached a signal-to-noise ratio of 12.5 across 94 nights of observing, a clean confirmation that intensity mapping can carry cosmological information without leaning on any other telescope. The detection matters because it removes a crutch that earlier 21cm cosmology work could not do without. To pick a faint hydrogen signal out of the radio sky, every previous CHIME result had to be cross-correlated with an external galaxy or quasar catalog, so that any structure showing up in both maps could be trusted. That technique works, but it ties a hydrogen experiment to the schedule and depth of someone else’s survey. The instrument has been collecting data continuously since first light in 2017 and the collaboration says it now has nearly seven years of observations in hand, most of which has not yet been analyzed. If the new processing pipeline can keep extracting the auto-power spectrum cleanly from older data, CHIME should be able to push the measurement to higher redshifts, into the period when the universe was only about three billion years old, and to lower redshifts, where the dark-energy signal is strongest. The first detection was a 2023 paper that cross-correlated CHIME’s hydrogen maps with optical galaxy and quasar catalogs from eBOSS. The team reads the gap between observation and simulation as a clue about how tightly hydrogen is packed at the small, non-linear scales the new measurement is most sensitive to, not as evidence that the total hydrogen inventory is wrong. Foreground-removal eliminates some of the largest-scale modes the BAO analysis needs, and the detected power spectrum occupies smaller non-linear scales where gravitational clustering has already scrambled the clean linear signal. The next step is to apply that capability across more of the CHIME archive and across the wider redshift range the telescope was built for. For a community that has spent more than a decade waiting for a 21cm cosmology result that does not need a galaxy survey attached, the message from the Okanagan Valley this week is that the wait is over, and the next decade of dark-energy measurements just got a new instrument.

withheld.headline: A Distant Planet Emitted a Burst of Radio Waves. Why? - Nautilus
withheld.evidence: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. evaluation.strongest_fact: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion‑year‑old millisecond signal from space More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. Finding a Radio Signal from 10 Billion Years Ago We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. withheld.headline: FoN Campaign Defends Ghana's Expanded Fishing Zone
withheld.evidence: Government has doubled Ghana's Inshore Exclusive Zone from six to 12 nautical miles for artisanal fishers — now Friends of the Nation is training coastal communities in Ahanta West to stop trawlers from crossing the new line. Barely days after a canoe fisherman in Butre spoke of his fears that marine protection rules could push small-scale operators further out to sea, an environmental NGO has launched a campaign aimed at making sure the opposite happens — that industrial trawlers, not artisanal canoes, are kept out of protected waters. Friends of the Nation (FoN) launched its "Protecting Our Zone, Securing Our Future" campaign at a day-long workshop held in Upper and Lower Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality of the Western Region on 11 October 2026, according to the Ghana News Agency (GNA). The workshop brought together fishers, fishmongers and other industry stakeholders to explain recent regulatory changes and the boundaries of Ghana's newly expanded Inshore Exclusive Zone (IEZ). The IEZ is a stretch of sea reserved exclusively for canoe fishers and other small-scale, artisanal operators, where larger industrial vessels are barred from casting nets. According to FoN, government has extended this protected zone from six nautical miles to 12 nautical miles offshore, effectively doubling the area set aside for Ghana's coastal fishing communities. Mevuta Donkris, FoN's Executive Director, thanked government for the extension but cautioned that the new boundary would only mean something if fishers themselves remained alert, GNA reports. A security researcher says data presented at a regional meeting in Senegal shows about 2,000 illegal migrants entered Ghana between March 2025 and July 2026, renewing calls for stronger border controls. withheld.headline: Mark Dennis went from top silk and charity 'big boss' to accused predator
withheld.evidence: Mark Dennis built a reputation defending accused criminals before he himself became the accused. ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon ) Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide. There is a small terrace house in Sydney's inner west that always gave builder Chad Loxsom an uneasy feeling. "I've been in thousands and thousands of people's houses," he said, but this one "was a little bit strange". The Leichhardt property belonged to Mark Dennis SC, a criminal defence barrister, who Loxsom said had a "weird demeanour" and was "just odd". But what he saw inside is what gnawed at him for years. "All over the walls of his house, he had dozens upon dozens upon dozens of pictures of him with little kids," he said. The electrician first noticed the "come back with a warrant" doormat, and then the large mirror fixed to the ceiling above Dennis's bed. Dennis was found dead in his home in Sydney's inner west in February. What was found on his devices led to his arrest, a raid of his house, and child abuse material charges from evidence prosecutors described as "disturbing". Dennis was released on bail, and soon after, was found dead in his home . Last week, Background Briefing and ABC Investigations revealed his death did not bring the police investigation to an end . The ABC travelled to Cambodia in June to retrace Dennis's steps to reveal the inside story of how an accused predator accumulated power within a high-profile charity and gained access to vulnerable children. In an investigation that combines a tranche of internal documents with dozens of interviews, the ABC can reveal allegations that Dennis sexually harassed a former Sunrise staff member and made teenage girls feel uncomfortable by excessive touching. The charity defended its child protection policies, saying the children always came first. Maggie Eno runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Eno, who did not want to comment on Sunrise specifically, said sponsors should never have access to children because criminals were "sophisticated" and "always" had the goal of getting "direct access to the children".
